title: The universal form
hook: Arjuna is given a divine eye to see Krishna's universal form, and among the faces rushing into it are names the blind king knows.
carry: god is everything, yet comes as a friend

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna argued, and Krishna answered with karma yoga and a promise to come age after age. Your line: karma yoga: work as an offering, not for the prize.

Two people in this story are given eyes they weren't born with. One is Sanjaya, who sees the whole battlefield from the palace so he can tell the king. The other is Arjuna, who in the eleventh chapter of the Gita asks to see Krishna as he truly is, and is told his ordinary eyes can't do it. So Krishna gives him a divine eye. And then there's us, listening, because the one describing Arjuna's vision is Sanjaya, speaking to a blind father. Session five of six: the vision, heard from inside the palace.
screen: `EYES THEY WEREN'T BORN WITH` → `ARJUNA GETS A DIVINE EYE` → `SANJAYA TELLS THE BLIND KING`

segments.voice: Arjuna sees a form with countless faces and eyes, a light like a thousand suns rising at once, the whole universe gathered in one body. And remember who's telling it: Sanjaya, to a blind father. Then the vision turns. Arjuna sees the warriors rushing into terrible mouths, like rivers racing to the sea, like moths into a flame. The sons of Dhritarashtra. Bhishma. Drona. Karna. Our own warriors too. The blind king hears his own sons among them. Arjuna, shaking, asks: who are you? Krishna answers: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds. Be only the instrument. At the end, terrified, Arjuna asks to see his friend's familiar face again. Krishna takes his gentle form, and Arjuna says: now I'm myself again. Krishna adds that only loving devotion lets a person see him truly. Hindus call this vision the vishvarupa, the universal form: God as the whole universe, the light and the life, even time and death. And yet the same God comes back as a friend with a face. Here's the big teaching. Many Hindus worship one infinite God through forms they can love: a murti on the home shrine, baby Krishna with butter on his hands, the charioteer at the reins. Many teachers read this chapter as the reason. The infinite is real, and too much to hold. The familiar face isn't a smaller god. It's the door.
screen: `A THOUSAND SUNS AT ONCE` · `I AM TIME. BE THE INSTRUMENT.` · `THE FAMILIAR FACE AGAIN` · then, large: `VISHVARUPA: GOD AS EVERYTHING`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep a small murti or picture of God at home. Let your gaze go soft and widen your attention: the room, the street, the sky over it, everything at once. Then come back, gently, to one familiar thing: the picture on your shrine if you have one, or a cup, or your own hand. Stay there. If you pray, let that familiar face be your door to the infinite. If you don't, notice how the near thing steadies you.
Bhishma Parva. The book whose grandsire stands in the ranks while Arjuna's vision of everything names him among those Time has already taken.
Your line: God is everything, yet comes as a friend. A thousand suns, then a familiar face. That's day eight hundred twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 823 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A BLESSING BEFORE THE BATTLE.`

howItsDone: The vision of the universal form, the vishvarupa, in the Gita's eleventh chapter is read and recited, and appears in temple art and posters showing Krishna with many faces and arms before Arjuna's chariot, beside the gentler forms most homes keep on the shrine.
